newsitem.title: UK: Arguments rage in copper market over "hidden" stockpile.
newsitem.headline: Arguments rage in copper market over "hidden" stockpile.

text.p: The opaque world of metals trading has been rattled in the wake of the Sumitomo scandal by reports that up to half a million tonnes of copper may be stashed in hidden stockpiles.

On Wednesday, the UK-based World Bureau of Metal Statistics (WBMS) estimated that nearly 600,000 tonnes of copper not previously reported may have built up in Netherlands bonded warehouses between 1991 and 1995.
On the London Metal Exchange (LME) copper prices fell, even though many traders said there is no such stockpile.
"It does just not exist - I would be reluctant to say that it is impossible, but the chances of it are so small," a senior trader said.
Merchant traders, who often form the link between copper producers and consumers by holding surplus metal, agreed, citing the current undersupplied nature of the physical market.
Refined copper warehouse stocks registered by the LME are at 109,175 tonnes - the lowest since September 1990, and there is also a shortage of lower-grade copper cathode as well as scrap.

Because of this, the cash price on the LME is at a $70/75 premium or backwardation to the three months level. If there was some "hidden' copper around it would be delivered on the LME to take advantage of the backwardation, industry sources said.
"I do not think there is even 1,000 tonnes of hidden stocks in the Netherlands," one leading merchant said.
Another industry analyst said that it would be virtually impossible to hide away half a million tonnes of copper for any period of time.
"I have been to European smelters who hold say 20,000 tonnes of stock. That takes up a tremendous amount of space, so I cannot imagine what 20 times that would take up," he said.
However, the LME price has been rattled by the implications, with three months metal trading down to $2,020 a tonne on Thursday, against Wednesday's two-month peaks of $2,083.
The possibility that sizeable tonnages of copper have been and may still be hidden from various reporting agencies explains some of the imponderables the 1990s threw up.
Switching copper between the highly-visible LME warehouses and secretive off-market stores may have allowed Sumitomo Corp's former head trader Yasuo Hamanaka to operate without discovery for years.

In June, Sumitomo fired Hamanaka after it alleged that he admitted running up losses now put at $2.6 billion in 10 years of unauthorised trading. Hamanaka has since been arrested and charged with fraud.

"There is metal disappearing off the LME and it is clearly not going into consumption. The market cannot go from showing a small surplus to major deficit in a month. Something strange is happening to the LME stocks," Peter Hollands of Bloomsbury Minerals Economics said.
Independent analyst Simon Hunt noted that data from the WBMS was to the end of 1995, when the market was different from now.
"You do not get metal staying off-warrant in a backwardation. There was some hidden inventory associated with Hamanaka, and it probably was around 100,000 tonnes. It has now disappeared," he said.

A European industry source said the divergence in the data between 1991/95 LME figures and the Netherlands Dutch Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS) numbers, on which the WBMS report was based, was due to trade flows.

"By comparing the statistics given by Dutch CBS which include all copper coming through Rotterdam which is the gateway to Europe and includes copper going straight through to consumers against the LME stock figures you come to this wrong conclusion," he said.
There are also question marks against data from the former Soviet Union, which is hightly unreliable.
"Rotterdam is the major receiver of copper from Russia and Kazakhstan. It may well be registered as copper coming in, but in reality it could be propellers going out," the senior trader said.
Because of the bulk of FSU material imported into Europe - over one million tonnes between 1991 and 1994 - this may be part of the discrepancy.
